Day 1: Imran did his maths homework at the desk with the tablet propped beside the pencil box. Every few minutes his eyes slid sideways to the screen. Forty minutes of sums took ninety. His sister Noor peeped in and said, “Even I look at mine. It's just how the screen pulls.”

Day 3: Noor put the tablet on the shelf in the hall. Imran did sums in forty-five minutes, humming.

Day 6: The tablet was at his elbow again, dark. He touched it once, sighed, and slid it to the far side of the desk.

qa.q: Who moved the tablet to the shelf in the hall?
qa.a: Noor put the tablet on the shelf in the hall.

qa.q: How can you tell that Imran wanted to look at the tablet on Day 6?
qa.a: Imran touched it once and sighed, which shows the pull was still there and he felt tempted, but he moved it away.

qa.q: What difference did the tablet's place make between Day 1 and Day 3?
qa.a: With the tablet out of reach, forty minutes of sums took forty-five, not ninety, so the homework went faster.

qa.q: How might Noor see Imran's glances at the screen?
qa.a: Noor sees them as ordinary, saying even Noor looks at a phone or screen during homework, and does not blame Imran.

grounding: A schoolchild does homework with a screen within reach and takes twice as long, because novelty pulls attention.

passage: “You keep glancing at that phone, Chetan. Come here and listen. I'm Varun, and when I was ten, there was a radio in the next room, and my father listened to the cricket commentary with the door open. I sat at my table with the algebra and heard every ball. I wrote a line, I heard a cheer, I wrote half a line, I listened. What should have been half an hour took two. My mother came in, saw my face, and said, 'It isn't that you're bad at this, it's that a cheer is louder than a sum.' She picked up my book and my pencil and moved me to the kitchen, where the radio was faint. I finished in twenty minutes.”

qa.a: The radio was playing the cricket commentary.

qa.q: How did the ten-year-old Varun feel listening to each cheer?
qa.a: Varun felt torn and pulled, because the cheers kept drawing attention away from the sums, and the half-lines show it.

qa.q: What choice by the mother changed the evening?
qa.a: The mother moved Varun and the book to the kitchen, where the radio was faint, and Varun finished in twenty minutes.

qa.q: How might the mother have felt seeing Varun's face?
qa.a: The mother probably felt sympathetic and practical, since she said it was not that Varun was bad at algebra but that a cheer was louder than a sum.

grounding: A schoolchild studies with a noisy distraction near and takes far longer, because the brain is pulled by novelty.

passage: The after-school study room at the hostel had one television, mounted high in the corner, and today it showed a cricket match. Mohit, eleven, had fifteen maths sums. He sat at the table nearest the TV. He solved one, looked up at the screen. Solved another. A boundary was hit; everyone cheered, and Mohit forgot what seven times eight was. By dinner he had done eight sums. Naveen sir, the warden, noticed. "Mohit, tomorrow sit at the back table, facing the wall." The next evening Mohit finished all fifteen in forty minutes and was surprised that it had been so quick.

qa.q: How many maths sums did Mohit have?
qa.a: Mohit had fifteen maths sums.

qa.q: How did Mohit feel the next evening after finishing quickly?
qa.a: He felt surprised and probably pleased that the sums had gone so fast once the television was behind him.

qa.q: What did Naveen sir do well?
qa.a: He changed where Mohit sat instead of scolding him, which removed the screen from view.

qa.q: How might Naveen sir see Mohit's slow progress on the first evening?
qa.a: Naveen sir probably saw that the TV kept pulling Mohit's attention, not that he was lazy, and chose a practical fix.

grounding: Shows a schoolchild glancing at a nearby screen and taking longer, then finishing faster once it is out of view.

passage:
Monday. Chaitanya, ten, did his English homework on the sofa while his mother Seema's phone played videos next to him. Every few minutes he glanced over. Two pages of writing took him an hour and a half.
Wednesday. Seema noticed and put the phone in her bedroom while he worked at the dining table. He grumbled. "I wasn't even watching." Still, he finished in forty-five minutes.
Saturday. Chaitanya set up the table himself, without being asked, and asked her to take the phone to her room. "It's quicker," he said. He finished his worksheet and went out to play before lunch, looking pleased.

qa.q: Where did Chaitanya do his homework on Monday?
qa.a: He did his English homework on the sofa.

qa.q: Why did Chaitanya grumble on Wednesday?
qa.a: He felt a little defensive and annoyed, insisting he wasn't even watching, not yet seeing how the phone slowed him.

qa.q: Which change helped, and why?
qa.a: Moving the phone to the bedroom and working at the dining table removed the screen's pull, halving his homework time.

qa.q: How might Seema feel on Saturday?
qa.a: Seema would likely feel pleased and proud that Chaitanya set up the table himself and asked for the phone to be moved.

grounding: Shows across days a child whose homework takes twice as long with a screen nearby, and faster once it is moved away.

subtype: Homework with phone or TV near [Actor]
passage: Uma, beta, sit, I'll tell you about your father when he was nine. We had just got our first television, black and white. Hemant would do his homework on the floor right in front of it, and I'd hear, "Just one minute, Amma, just this song." Two pages of arithmetic took him all evening. I scolded, and it didn't help. He wasn't being naughty; the moving pictures simply pulled his eyes. One day his teacher sent a note home. That evening, I moved his books to the verandah, far from the TV, and sat with my knitting. He finished in half an hour and then ran to watch his programme, guilt-free.

qa.q: What kind of television did they first get?
qa.a: They got a black and white television.

qa.q: How did Hemant feel when he could finish on the verandah?
qa.a: He likely felt relieved and free, finishing in half an hour and then watching his programme without guilt.

qa.q: Which choice in the story worked better than scolding?
qa.a: Moving Hemant's books to the verandah, far from the TV, worked where scolding had not.

qa.q: How did the elder come to see Hemant's behaviour?
qa.a: The elder came to see that he wasn't being naughty; the moving pictures just pulled his eyes, so changing the place made more sense than scolding.

grounding: An elder tells how a child's homework dragged with a TV nearby, and how moving away from it helped.

subtype: Homework with phone or TV near [Actor]
passage:
The family's one-room house had a single light and a single television, and on Thursday night it was showing the cricket final. Kamal's maths test was the next morning.
He sat on the mat with his notebook, back to the screen. Every roar from the crowd made him turn. Six! He turned. Wicket! He turned. He did one sum, watched an over, then lost his place on the second.
At the drinks break, his big brother Lalit asked, "How many sums?"
"Two." It had been an hour.
Lalit moved Kamal's mat and the lamp to the verandah and pulled the curtain across the door. "Your brain isn't lazy. It just can't ignore a six."
On the verandah, Kamal finished the other eight sums in forty minutes. Lalit told him the final score afterwards.

qa.q: How many sums had Kamal done after an hour?
qa.a: Two.

qa.q: How did Kamal feel when each roar came from the television?
qa.a: Kamal felt torn and restless, turning his head at every six and wicket and losing his place in the sums.

qa.q: What did Lalit change that helped, and why?
qa.a: Lalit moved Kamal's mat and lamp to the verandah and pulled the curtain, removing the screen instead of blaming Kamal.

qa.q: How does Lalit see Kamal's distraction?
qa.a: Lalit sees it as normal, not laziness, saying Kamal's brain just can't ignore a six.

grounding: Shows a child doing homework with a cricket match on nearby who keeps glancing at it, until the screen is moved out of view.
